new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Re-opened (the PDF's metadata gives the title 'An Initial Appreciation of the Dialect Situation in Saluan and Batui (Eastern Sulawesi, Indonesia)', authors David Mead and Edy Pasanda, 136 pp., SIL ESR 2015-013). Appendix B.1 item (a) is at PDF p.36 = book p.29 exactly as quoted: 'In general, stress is non-phonemic, occurring on the penultimate syllable (but see the discussion below concerning long vowels, where indication of stress is significant).' Item (d) at PDF p.37 = book p.30 exactly as quoted: 'Long vowels are distinctive in that they do not attract stress, which falls on the preceding (viz. penultimate) syllable; and they cannot be followed by a consonant.' with examples ˈsiku 'elbo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable and is not contrastive. A word-final long vowel (V:) counts as one syllable and does not attract stress (ˈʔikuː 'tail', ˈsiku 'elbow'), whereas a geminate double vowel counts as two syllables so stress lands on its first mora (tuˈmuːʔ). The Batui (Tolando) wordlist in Appendix B is transcribed accordingly: 489 of 534 stress-marked Batui forms are penultimate by vowel count; the remainder are monosyllables (ˈsuːŋ, ˈhoːn) and final long/geminate-vowel + consonant forms (kasuˈbiːʔ, ʔoˈhiːʔ) that fit the geminate-VV-as-two-syllables analysis.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is marked in the wordlists when heard (e.g. Batui ˌbulunuˈmata 'eyelashes', ˌʔanumpuˈleːʔ); no rule is stated, but the marked forms show it on alternating syllables to the left of primary stress in compounds/longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Statement is hedged 'in general'; item (i) p.31 warns that differences in stress placement across wordlists may reflect mistranscription; the long-vowel vs geminate-vowel analysis (d) is stated explicitly for Saluan, and §3.1 notes Batui has lost length in some lexemes where Saluan keeps it.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited in a 200/489-item wordlist; not a phonology sketch. The statement is made jointly for the eleven Saluan and one Batui wordlist rather than for Batui alone; the Batui evidence is the consistently penultimate stress marking of the TLD (Tolando, 2006, D. Mead) list.
new_statements.identity_note: Batui = batu1260 / zbt, formerly 'Baha' and wrongly treated as a Pamona dialect (Adriani & Kruyt 1914); the source's Batui data come from a single wordlist recorded at Tolando village, Batui district (Banggai regency) on 26-07-2006 by D. Mead. The stress remark in Appendix B.1 (a) is framed for all twelve Saluan-and-Batui wordlists together, and the long-vowel/stress analysis in B.1 (d) is stated for Saluan (salu1253/salu1252); Batui's fit is shown by the transcribed Batui forms, not by a Batui-specific sentence.
